bib.title: Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Beyond a Million Tokens: Benchmarking and Enhancing Long-Term Memory in LLMs", Mohammad Tavakoli, Alireza Salemi, Carrie Ye, Mohamed Abdalla, Hamed Zamani, J. Ross Mitchell (U Alberta, UMass Amherst). Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026 (arXiv:2510.27246v2, 21 Feb 2026). Introduces the BEAM benchmark and the LIGHT memory framework. Code and data: github.com/mohammadtavakoli78/BEAM.

COVERAGE: The PDF has 87 pages and 318,191 chars. I read the main text (pp.1-11) in full, and the appendix results in full: Tables 2-13 and Figures 3-5. I also read the case study (App. F) and the error analysis (App. G). I skimmed the reference list and the Appendix H prompts (Listings 1-44, which are generation templates, not results), and read only the key-value, scratchpad and filter prompts. I did not read Appendix B.3 (algorithms), D (nugget examples) or E (example dialogues) line by line. Not every page was read in full. No extraction faults.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- Claim: Every model degrades as dialogue length grows. Plain long-context models (up to 1M-token windows) average 0.104-0.133 at 10M, compared with 0.24-0.28 at 100K.
  number: Qwen vanilla 0.280 (100K) -> 0.133 (10M); Llama-4-Maverick 0.240 -> 0.104; Gemini-2.0-flash 0.242 -> 0.122; GPT-4.1-nano 0.239 -> 0.109 (my reading of Table 1 averages)
  setup: BEAM, 4 lengths (100K/500K/1M/10M), 4 backbones, vanilla = whole history in context. At 10M no model fits, so each sees "the largest recent dialogue segment fitting their window". Qwen vanilla uses a 128K window.
  quote: "even LLMs with 1M token context windows (with and without retrieval-augmentation) struggle as dialogues lengthen."
  where: Abstract, p.1; Table 1, p.8

- Claim: LIGHT gives its largest gains over vanilla long-context at long lengths. Gains are relative and the headline numbers are measured against vanilla, not against the best baseline.
  number: +49.1% (Llama-4-Maverick) and +44.3% (GPT-4.1-nano) at 100K; +75.9% (GPT-4.1-nano) and +60.1% (Qwen) at 1M; +155.7% (Llama-4-Maverick) and +107.3% (GPT-4.1-nano) at 10M
  setup: Table 1 averages over 10 abilities. Qwen at 1M is 0.193 vanilla vs 0.309 LIGHT. Percentages are relative (my arithmetic matches).
  quote: "The benefits grow with context length: at 1M tokens, improvements reach +75.9% for GPT-4.1-nano and +60.1% for Qwen2.5-32B. At 10M tokens—where no baseline natively supports the full context—our method achieves dramatic improvements, including +155.7% for Llama-4-Maverick and +107.3% for GPT-4.1-nano."
  where: Sec 4.2, p.8

- Claim: Against the stronger RAG baseline the margin is small, a few points of absolute score. Averages from Table 1:
  number: 100K Qwen RAG 0.269 vs LIGHT 0.311; Llama 0.323 vs 0.358; GPT-4.1-nano 0.309 vs 0.345. At 10M: Qwen 0.211 vs 0.238; Llama 0.249 vs 0.266; GPT-4.1-nano 0.218 vs 0.226; Gemini 0.216 vs 0.192 (LIGHT loses)
  setup: RAG = each user-assistant turn pair embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5, FAISS, top-5. LIGHT = same retriever (k=5) plus scratchpad and working memory.
  quote: "Our method improves the LLM's performance in answering the probing questions by 3.5%–12.69% on average over the best-performing baseline, depending on the backbone model and conversation length."
  where: Sec 1, p.2; Table 1, p.8. The Gemini-at-10M exception is on p.8 ("slightly trails RAG, likely due to model-specific retrieval behavior").

- Claim: Ablation on Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ. The value of each LIGHT component rises with length. At 10M, removing any one costs 3.7 to 8.5 points. At 100K-1M, removing working memory slightly helps.
  number: 10M full 0.238 vs w/o retrieval 0.153, w/o scratchpad 0.202, w/o working memory 0.181, w/o noise filtering 0.155. At 100K full 0.311 vs w/o working memory 0.327. At 1M 0.309 vs 0.328.
  setup: Table 8, Qwen only. The text's drops are absolute points.
  quote: "By 10M, all components are essential, with removals leading to large drops (–8.5% for retrieval, –3.7% for scratchpad, –5.7% for working memory, –8.3% for noise filtering)."
  where: p.9; Table 8, p.30

- Claim: Retrieval budget k=15 beats the default k=5, and k=20 does not improve on it. k=10 is unreliable at 10M.
  number: LIGHT averages for k=5/10/15/20: 100K 0.311/0.321/0.334/0.325; 500K 0.316/0.321/0.350/0.350; 1M 0.309/0.325/0.330/0.330; 10M 0.238/0.171/0.253/0.245
  setup: Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ (inferred from the appendix intro, which states Qwen for the ablations; Table 9 does not name the model). Table 9. Text figures are relative gains.
  quote: "Performance consistently improves when increasing K from 5 to 15, with the best results at K=15 (+7.39%, +10.75%, +6.79%, and +6.3% at 100K, 500K, 1M, and 10M). Increasing further to K=20 slightly degrades performance, likely due to noisy context."
  where: p.9; Table 9, p.31. Note: the 500K and 1M averages tie at k=15 and k=20, so "slightly degrades" holds only at 100K and 10M.

- Claim: Sparse retrieval (SPLADE) helps slightly at up to 1M. Dense retrieval is better at 10M.
  number: +1.7% at 100K, +0.7% at 500K, +0.8% at 1M, -0.7% at 10M (absolute: 0.328 vs 0.311, and so on)
  setup: Qwen reader (Table 10 base values match the Qwen ablation); LIGHT with dense bge-small vs SPLADE-v2.
  quote: "SPLADE yields performance gains of 1.7% at 100K tokens, 0.7% at 500K, and 0.8% at 1M, but results in a slight performance drop of 0.7% at 10M."
  where: App C.2, p.31

- Claim: The ability profile is uneven. Gains are largest on summarization, preference following, information extraction and instruction following. All methods are best on abstention and worst on contradiction resolution (about 0.01-0.05 for everyone).
  number: summarization +160.6%, preference following +76.5%, information extraction +56.7%, temporal reasoning +56.3%, instruction following +39.5%, multi-hop +27.2%
  setup: Relative gains, aggregated across models and lengths.
  quote: "all methods—including ours—perform strongest in abstention and weakest in contradiction resolution, indicating that contradiction detection remains a challenging open problem."
  where: p.8-9

- Claim: On abstention, LIGHT is often worse than plain RAG and sometimes worse than vanilla. Examples:
  number: GPT-4.1-nano at 100K: RAG 0.800 vs LIGHT 0.575. Qwen at 500K: 0.728 vs 0.571. Qwen at 10M: 0.600 vs 0.550.
  setup: Table 1.
  quote: none beyond the table. The error analysis, App G, says the main abstention failure is that "the context contains information about entities, dates, or concepts that are similar to, but not the same as, the information requested".
  where: Table 1, p.8; App G, p.48

- Claim: A stronger embedding model helps LIGHT more than it helps RAG.
  number: GPT-4.1-nano LIGHT average at 10M: bge-small 0.226 vs bge-large 0.263. RAG: 0.218 vs 0.231. At 1M: LIGHT 0.336 vs 0.343, RAG 0.302 vs 0.292.
  setup: Table 11, GPT-4.1-nano reader. The text's "16.37%" at 10M appears to be relative (0.263/0.226).
  quote: "achieving an additional 2.08% improvement at the 1M-token setting and 16.37% at the 10M-token setting."
  where: App C.3, p.33

- Claim: Index type has little effect (FlatIP vs HNSWFlat): 100K 0.345/0.347, 500K 0.335/0.325, 1M 0.336/0.324, 10M 0.226/0.237.
  setup: GPT-4.1-nano reader (Table 12).
  where: App C.4, p.33-34

- Claim: LIGHT beats ReadAgent (Lee et al., 2024) at every length.
  number: ReadAgent vs LIGHT averages: 100K 0.206 vs 0.311; 500K 0.191 vs 0.316; 1M 0.186 vs 0.309; 10M 0.148 vs 0.238. ReadAgent is better on abstention (e.g. 0.850 vs 0.475 at 100K).
  setup: Table 13. The reader is not named in the table; presumably Qwen, given the LIGHT column matches the Qwen numbers.
  where: App C.5, p.34-35

- Claim: The scratchpad adds value mainly by holding consolidated facts, standing instructions, overrides and normalised dates. Without it the model abstains or answers with the stale value.
  number: none (qualitative). Examples: "April 5, 2024" with the scratchpad vs "April 1, 2024" without; a 5-day difference vs 37 days.
  quote: "removing the scratchpad consistently causes failures that the full model avoids."
  where: App F, p.46-47

- Claim: The dominant knowledge-update and event-ordering failures come from the retriever, which returns documents by similarity and not in time order.
  number: none
  quote: "the retrieval model retrieves based on similarity, which does not necessarily preserve temporal order"
  where: App G, p.48. Also: on contradiction resolution the model "overweighs one side of the contradiction due to position and frequency bias".

- Claim: BEAM is 100 conversations and 2,000 validated questions, with 20 probes per conversation (2 per ability). Conversation quality ratings were about 4.5-4.6 on average.
  number: Human ratings: Coherence 4.53, Realism 4.57, Complexity 4.64 (1-5 scale). Cohen's kappa on 20 conversations: 0.7044, 0.7391, 0.7849. Lengths: 100K to 10M. 10 abilities, of which 3 are new (instruction following, event ordering, contradiction resolution).
  setup: Two annotators with CS backgrounds, who read only about 25 turns at the start, middle and end of each conversation plus random turns.
  quote: "The average scores across all conversations were 4.53, 4.57, and 4.64, respectively, indicating consistently high quality."
  where: p.10; App B.2, p.18-19

LIGHT design details (for the note)
- Three memories. Episodic is a retrieval index over per-turn key-value facts plus a summary, embedded with bge-small-en-v1.5, with the original dialogue segments as values. Working memory is the last z dialogue pairs. The scratchpad is a running set of salient facts that is not stored in a vector DB but fed directly to the prompt.
- Scratchpad compression: "once content exceeds a 30K-token threshold—substantially shorter than the raw conversation—it is compressed into a 15K-token summary by GPT-4.1-nano". Extraction runs with Qwen2.5-32B-AWQ after every turn pair.
- At query time the scratchpad is semantically chunked. Qwen gives a yes/no relevance label per chunk, and only the "yes" chunks are kept. This is the "noise filtering" component.
- The compression prompt has a rule to "Eliminate older values when there is newer and updated value for a thing", and uses fixed section headings (KEY ENTITIES, USER INSTRUCTIONS, IMPORTANT DATES, and so on).
  where: Sec 3, p.6-7; Listings in App H, pp.85-86

LIMITS
- The authors' own caveats are thin. There is no formal limitations section.
- Conversations are synthetic: user turns are written by Llama-3.3-70B and the probes by GPT-4.1/4.1-mini. Human validation covered probes and rubrics. Quality checks read only samples of each conversation (about 25 turns at the start, middle and end plus random turns).
- Scoring is LLM-judged against nuggets (0, 0.5 or 1). Event ordering uses Kendall tau-b with an LLM equivalence detector.
- At 10M no model sees the whole dialogue, so vanilla is handicapped to its most recent window. Llama-4-Scout, the only model with a 10M window, was not tested ("extreme computational requirements").
- 10M scores come from few questions: 20 probes per conversation, so noise is high. Several 10M numbers are 0.000-0.050.
- The Gemini-2.0-flash 10M exception (see Claims).
- Several models are small or older (Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-4.1-nano, Gemini-2.0-flash), so the findings have dated. No frontier reasoning models were tested.
- Percent units are mixed: gains vs baselines and k are relative, while ablation and retriever deltas are absolute points.
- Table 10 has a typo ("0.43" for Contradiction Resolution at 100K, SPLADE).
- The ablations, k-sweep and retriever tests use one reader (Qwen). The embedding and index tests use GPT-4.1-nano.
- Contradiction resolution stays near zero for all systems, so LIGHT does not solve it.
- LIGHT's per-turn extraction cost (an LLM call per turn for key-values and the scratchpad) is not quantified.
- Single runs; no variance or confidence intervals are reported.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
- Binder & Desai 2011 and Sridhar et al. 2023 (cognitive-science inspiration for episodic, working and semantic memory); Teyler & DiScenna 1986 (hippocampal indexing).
- RAG: Lewis et al. 2020; HippoRAG (Jimenez Gutierrez et al. 2024); ReadAgent (Lee et al. 2024) as a baseline.
- Benchmarks it extends: LoCoMo (Maharana et al. 2024), LongMemEval (Zhong et al. 2024 as cited), MSC (Xu et al. 2021), DialSim (Kim et al. 2024a), MemoryBank, DuLeMon (Xu et al. 2022), PerLTQA (Du et al. 2024), MemBench (Tan et al. 2025), MemoryCode (Rakotonirina et al. 2025).
- Nugget evaluation: Pradeep et al. 2024, 2025. Kendall 1945 (tau-b). SPLADE v2 (Formal et al. 2022). FAISS (Douze et al. 2024). Kalai et al. 2025 (why models hallucinate, cited for abstention failures).

CODE: No code in the paper. The prompts in App H are the load-bearing artifacts: key-value extraction, scratchpad compression with fixed headings, the yes/no scratchpad filter, and the answer prompt with "Answer ONLY based on the provided context". Pages 85-87.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p.6): LIGHT architecture. Index and retrieval path, scratchpad path, and working-memory buffer feeding one prompt. This is the fastest way to explain the three-memory design.
- Fig 3 (p.9): ablation bars per length. It shows components mattering more as length grows.
- Fig 4 (p.9): retrieval budget k vs score.
- Fig 5 (p.32): dense vs SPLADE.
- Fig 1 (p.3): BEAM generation pipeline.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The text extraction is clean, but the tables are flattened, so bolding that marks the best score is lost (e.g. "0.3000.650" runs two numbers together). Verify Table 1 cell values against the PDF before quoting precise cells. The extraction did not label the reader in Tables 9, 10 and 13, so I inferred Qwen from matching values.

Extraction saved at /tmp/tav.txt (a scratch copy; not a report file).
